paragraphs.heading: The era of new life
paragraphs.text: The Cenozoic is the geological era we live in now, covering the last 66 million years of Earth's history. It is the most recent of the three eras of the Phanerozoic Eon, coming after the Paleozoic and the Mesozoic. Its name means "new life", from the Ancient Greek kainós, "new", and zōḗ, "life". British geologist John Phillips proposed the name in 1840, first spelling it Kainozoic, and it pairs with the earlier Mesozoic ("middle life") and Paleozoic ("old life").

paragraphs.heading: The Age of Mammals
paragraphs.text: The era began with the Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction, when many species, including the non-avian dinosaurs, died out; most experts blame the impact of the Chicxulub asteroid or other body from space. With so many groups gone, mammals and birds diversified until large ones dominated life on Earth. That is why the Cenozoic is often called the Age of Mammals. Placental mammals ruled the land in the Northern Hemisphere and marsupials in the Southern Hemisphere, and insects, birds and flowering plants also mark the era.

paragraphs.heading: Periods and epochs
paragraphs.text: The Cenozoic has three periods, named the Paleogene, Neogene and Quaternary. These are further cut into seven epochs, running from the Paleocene to the Holocene. In 2004 the Paleogene and Neogene officially took the place of the older Tertiary Period, and the Quaternary was officially recognised in June 2009. Because its rocks are fairly young and well preserved, this era is known in more detail than any other. Epochs help palaeontologists sort its many important events.

paragraphs.heading: Moving continents, changing climate
paragraphs.text: The continents moved into their present positions during the Cenozoic. Early on they were taking their modern shape but all stood apart, India included; the Tethys Sea divided Afro-Eurasia, and the Americas were not yet joined at Panama. The early Cenozoic was warmer than today, especially during the Paleocene–Eocene Thermal Maximum. Later, the change from the Eocene to the Oligocene and the Quaternary glaciation made Earth cooler and drier.

paragraphs.heading: Forests and warmth
paragraphs.text: The Paleocene, from 66 to 56 million years ago, saw modern placental mammals arise. The loss of large plant-eaters let dense forests spread, usually with few species, and a warming trend eventually carried jungles to the poles. With the big sea reptiles gone, sharks ruled the oceans. In the Eocene, from 56 to 33.9 million years ago, early primates, whales and horses lived in dense forests. Carbon dioxide stood at about 1,400 ppm and the temperature was 30 degrees Celsius, with little difference from pole to pole.

paragraphs.heading: Cooling and grasslands
paragraphs.text: In the mid-Eocene a current formed between Australia and Antarctica, disrupting ocean circulation worldwide and cooling the globe, which shrank the jungles. Mammals then grew to huge sizes, among them whales that had become almost fully at home in water. The late Eocene brought back the seasons, and savanna-like land spread as grasses evolved. In the Oligocene, from 33.9 to 23.03 million years ago, spreading grasslands led to many new species, including the first elephants, cats and dogs.
